summary.title: Developing in Production
summary.one_liner: Developers can build and debug individual services safely inside production using traffic replay, isolated "playground" sandboxes, and stubbed dependencies, rather than trying to replicate a complex production environment locally or in staging.
takeaways: Staging and local replicas of complex distributed systems tend to be out of date and fail to reproduce emergent, scale-dependent behavior.
Separate deployments (artifacts) from releases (feature flags), and roll out gradually from one server to all servers.
Give each developer an ephemeral, isolated playground in production fed by a 'garden hose' of mirrored traffic, with limited read access and no write access to the wider system.
Handle dependencies with service virtualization, stubs, synthetic transactions, or datastore virtualization/materialization, and test one service at a time rather than end-to-end.
This approach only makes sense once you already have strong CI/CD, feature flags, observability and chaos engineering practices.
summary.summary: Will Sargent's essay argues that complex distributed systems exhibit emergent behavior that smaller staging or laptop replicas cannot reproduce, and that maintaining duplicate environments is costly and drifts out of date. He describes a testing-in-production workflow: feature flags, staged rollouts, and rollback, followed by a per-developer 'playground' service in production that receives replayed production traffic. The post surveys tools and patterns for this, including Goreplay, ShadowReader, Envoy traffic mirroring, and approaches for handling state and external dependencies. It also proposes a remote Linux workspace for developers, with the caveat that the model requires a mature operational setup.
